title: Data: Your Numbers Should Work Like a Clean Windshield
summary: A few weekly numbers, each with an owner, let leaders spot trouble early. Notes on the EOS book Data: testing gut feel, swapping hope for evidence, fewer surprises.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Data
book.originalTitle: Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable
book.note: This article is a practical reflection on the book within the EOS context. It is not a substitute for reading the original work.

html:
Monday, 9 a.m. The revenue dashboard is green. Sales says the pipeline "looks great." Ops says delivery is "getting better." Then finance mentions, almost in passing, that two big invoices are now 60 days late. Everyone in the room has numbers. Nobody has the same picture. You're driving in heavy rain with the wipers off, and the car is still doing 80.

That feeling is the starting point of Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable by Mark O'Donnell, Angela Kalemis and Mark Stanley. Its page on EOS Worldwide pitches it at leaders who feel lost about how the business is doing, get blindsided by things they didn't see coming, or lose sleep over whether the company will make it (EOS Worldwide). It's the deep dive on the Data Component of EOS, the Entrepreneurial Operating System, and it's the first book in this series of notes. My one-line version: data earns its place when it works like a clean windshield. It shows you the road ahead early enough to steer.

Fewer numbers, picked on purpose

When things feel foggy, the first instinct is to ask for more reports. Another tab in the spreadsheet, another chart on the dashboard. It rarely helps. Forty metrics on one screen leave the team with the same question it started with: what do we do this week?

EOS goes the other way. Its main tool is a weekly Scorecard with 5 to 15 Measurables. Each one has one owner and one weekly goal that defines "on track," and the team looks at 13 weeks side by side so it reacts to trends instead of a single bad week (EOS Scorecard). The same page says to start with activity-based numbers whenever you can. Those are the inputs that move before the results do: demos booked, proposals sent, orders shipped on time. Revenue at the end of the quarter tells you what already happened. Proposals sent this week tell you what's coming.

So a useful number passes a simple test. If it turns red, does someone know what to do on Monday? "Total leads" often fails that test. "Qualified demos booked by the sales team" usually passes, because it points at a person and an action.

Your gut is a good first witness

Founders run on instinct, and they should. Plenty of good calls get made before there's any data to back them. EOS doesn't ask you to drop that. Mike Paton puts it this way on the EOS Worldwide blog: raw instinct is extremely valuable, and the best decisions come when you temper it with real, objective data (Clear the Fog).

Mark O'Donnell, one of the book's three authors, uses an aviation picture for it in a post on the EOS blog. Intuition is the early-warning radar, data is the cockpit instruments. His closing line is the one I'd pin above my desk: "Intuition starts the conversation; data closes it." He also suggests a 30-day routine for testing a hunch. Write it in one sentence, turn it into something testable, pick 3 to 5 measures, pull rough data from whatever exports you already have, then bring the result to the weekly leadership meeting (Gut Feel vs. Hard Facts).

Say you have a hunch that customers who come through referrals stay longer. Nice hunch. Now it's a question with an answer: retention at 90 days, referral versus ads, over the last two quarters. If you're right, you move budget with confidence. If you're wrong, you just saved that budget.

Hope is not a metric

Every team has its hopeful sentences. "That big deal is basically done." "The client will pay next week." "The new process will settle down soon." Any of them might be true. The trouble starts when they stand in for evidence week after week.

This isn't a character flaw. It's how people plan. In "Delusions of Success," Dan Lovallo and Daniel Kahneman describe how executives fall for optimism when they forecast big projects: benefits get overestimated, costs and delays get underestimated, and many initiatives never deliver what the plan promised (Harvard Business Review, 2003). A weekly number doesn't make anyone less hopeful. It gives that hope something to check against.

The question I find most useful is short: if this is true, what should we see this week?

What you hear What you ask to see
"The pipeline is healthy." Deals that moved a stage this week, and how many are older than your usual sales cycle.
"That deal is almost signed." The next step, its date, and who on the client side has said yes.
"Delivery is getting better." On-time rate or rework count for the last few weeks, side by side.
"They'll pay soon." Days the invoice is overdue and the date the client committed to.

None of these questions accuses anyone. They just ask the good news to show up in a form everyone can see.

A number gives the room something to stand on

EOS splits the top of a company into two roles. The Visionary looks ahead: products, markets, the big relationships. The Integrator keeps the machine running: priorities, people, follow-through. Without numbers both drift into the wrong work. The Visionary starts checking every email because they can't tell how things are going. The Integrator spends the week putting out fires that a weekly number would have flagged a month ago.

The Scorecard gives both of them the same view. When a Measurable goes off track, it drops onto the Issues List and the team works it in the weekly meeting (EOS Scorecard). That changes the tone of hard conversations a lot. "I feel like sales is slipping" puts someone on the defensive. "Proposals sent have been under goal for three weeks. What do we think is going on?" puts a problem on the table and invites everyone to help. It's still a hard talk. It's a fairer one.

That only works when every number has a real owner who chose it, understands it and can move it. The third post in this series covers that part: Everyone has a number, and it isn't surveillance.

Fewer surprises, more room to lead

Measuring the right things doesn't make decisions easy. It makes fewer of them urgent. See cash getting tight in week 3, and you can sit down with the bank and plan. See it in week 11, and you're cutting costs in a panic. See delivery capacity shrinking early, and you can renegotiate scope before a client loses trust. See a sales number go red with half the quarter left, and the team can still fix it instead of explaining it.

That's the kind of freedom a good Data Component buys a leader. You stop holding the whole company in your head, because a one-page view holds the important parts for you. Cash gets its own post later in this series: revenue is not cash.

The idea I'm keeping

Data is a small set of numbers that lets the team see reality early enough to act. If a number never changes what anyone does, it's decoration, and you can take it off the page.

Try this week

  • Open your current dashboard and circle the numbers that changed a decision in the last month. Question every number you didn't circle.
  • For each circled number, write down one owner and one weekly goal.
  • Pick one hopeful sentence you heard this week and ask: if it's true, what should we see by Friday?
  • Write one hunch you have about the business in a single sentence, then choose 3 measures that would prove it right or wrong.
  • Sketch a one-page Monday view. If you looked at it for ten minutes, would you know what needs attention first?

Building that one-page view is the next step, and the next post in this series is about exactly that: a scorecard as a one-page early warning system.

faqs.q: What is the Data Component in EOS?
faqs.a: It's one of the six components of the EOS Model. In practice it means running the business on a handful of objective numbers, mostly through a weekly Scorecard of 5 to 15 Measurables, each with one owner and one weekly goal.

faqs.q: How many numbers should a leadership scorecard track?
faqs.a: EOS recommends 5 to 15, reviewed every week with 13 weeks visible side by side. Start with activity-based numbers such as proposals sent or demos booked, because they move before results like revenue do.

No. Mark O'Donnell, one of the book's three authors, calls intuition an early-warning radar and data the cockpit instruments: intuition starts the conversation and data closes it. Write the hunch down in one sentence, then pick 3 to 5 measures that would prove it right or wrong.

faqs.q: How do I question an optimistic update without sounding harsh?
faqs.a: Ask what you should see this week if the update is true: the next step and its date for a deal, days overdue for an invoice, the on-time rate for delivery. The question is about evidence, so nobody has to defend themselves.
